verdict.rationale: Two patterns that are heavy with specific Greek and Hebrew words stand in real tension, and the words by themselves do not rank one above the other. On one side, Matthew 5:39 places the verb 'to resist' or 'to set oneself against' (antistenai, G0436, in the aorist active infinitive, which is a completed-action verbal noun form) under a prohibition addressed to the disciple in the second person, illustrated by personal insult, lawsuit, and Roman forced-labor service (corvee, meaning compelled state labor). Matthew 5:44 then sets a present-tense command 'keep loving' (agapate) toward the 'enemy' or 'hostile person' (echthros). Romans 12:17-21 forbids 'paying back evil for evil' (apodidontes kakon anti kakou), reserves 'vengeance' or 'judicial payback' (ekdikesis, G1557) to God, and commands 'overcome evil with good' (nika en to agatho to kakon). Matthew 26:52 has Jesus tell the disciple 'put back the sword' (apostrepson ten machairan) with the warning 'those who take the sword' (hoi labontes machairan) 'will perish by the sword' (en machaira apolountai). On the other side, the same epistle one sentence later in Romans 13:4 calls the civil ruler 'God's servant' or 'minister' (theou diakonos) who 'does not bear the sword in vain' (ou eike ten machairan, G3162, phorei) as an 'avenger' or 'one who carries out justice' (ekdikos, G1558) 'for wrath' (eis orgen). The cognate verb 'to set oneself against' (antitassomai) and the perfect-tense 'has set himself against' (anthesteken, a completed action whose result still stands) in Romans 13:2 turn the very same anti-stem (the 'against'-root word family) into culpable resistance when it is aimed at the civil sphere. The Old Testament 'eye for eye' formula (lex talionis, the Latin name for that proportional-punishment rule) in Exodus 21:24, Leviticus 24:20, and Deuteronomy 19:21 is judicial language for judges, not personal payback, and Genesis 9:6 grounds civic capital justice in the image of God. The canon supplies both a non-retaliatory disciple ethic and a sanctioned civil sword, and the word forms (lemmas, meaning the dictionary base forms) do not by themselves settle whether the same person occupies both roles.

scripture.reasoning: 'Eye for eye and tooth for tooth' (ophthalmon anti ophthalmou kai odonta anti odontos) quotes the Old Testament 'eye for eye' formula (lex talionis, the Latin label for that proportional-punishment rule) in Exodus 21:24, Leviticus 24:20, and Deuteronomy 19:21. In its Old Testament setting the formula is judicial, given to magistrates as a proportional ceiling on civic punishment, not as a license for personal payback. Reading the citation against its Old Testament source clarifies that Jesus is not abolishing civic justice but addressing the disciple's personal posture, which is what the following verses unfold.

The prohibition 'do not resist the evil one' (me antistenai to ponero) uses the aorist active infinitive (a completed-action verbal-noun form) of 'to set oneself against' (anthistemi) under the negative particle 'not' (me), governing the disciple addressed in the second person. The grammar pairs with the dative articular noun (a noun with 'the' attached, in the 'to/for' grammatical form) 'to the evil one' (to ponero), which can mean either the evil one or the evil person. The four illustrations that follow are personal and sub-lethal (not deadly): the right-cheek slap, the inner garment (chiton) in court, the compelled mile, the borrower. The clause constrains personal retaliation. Whether it extends to the magistrate or to lethal force is left open by the grammar itself.

The present-tense command 'keep on loving your enemies' (agapate tous echthrous hymon) commands ongoing love of enemies, reversing the cited 'hatred of the enemy' (mishesis ton echthron). The construction is durative (continuing over time) not punctiliar (a single moment), and the object is plural and personal. A non-resistant reading takes this as a kingdom ethic that excludes lethal response from the disciple; a sphere-distinction reading (one that separates the disciple's private role from the magistrate's public role) takes it as compatible with restraining a violent neighbor for the protection of a third party. The base word 'to love' (agapao) does not by itself settle the use of force by ordained authority.

'Put your sword back in its place, for all who take the sword will perish by the sword' (apostrepson ten machairan sou eis ton topon autes, pantes gar hoi labontes machairan en machaira apolountai) is Jesus's own constraint on disciple sword use at the very moment force is offered in his defense. The aorist active imperative (a completed-action command) 'put back' (apostrepson) and the gnomic (proverb-like, stating a general truth) future 'will perish' (apolountai) express a standing maxim about who lives by the sword. The grammar weighs against a disciple deploying lethal force in the kingdom's name, although the maxim is general enough that a sphere-distinction reading restricts it to private vigilantism (taking justice into one's own hands outside lawful office).

'Repaying to no one evil for evil' (medeni kakon anti kakou apodidontes), with the present participle 'paying back' (apodidontes, an ongoing action) negated by 'to no one' (medeni), frames a categorical disciple ethic of non-recompense in kind. The 'against/for' (anti) structure echoes Matthew 5:38's 'eye for eye' formula (lex talionis) but inverts it for personal conduct. This verse begins the pivot that runs into Romans 13 and is the literary hinge the canon places between the non-retaliatory disciple ethic and the civil sword.

'Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath. For it is written, vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord' (me heautous ekdikountes, agapetoi, alla dote topon te orge. Gegraptai gar, emoi ekdikesis, ego antapodoso, legei Kurios). The middle-voice participle 'avenging yourselves' (ekdikountes, a self-directed ongoing action) is forbidden to the disciple, 'vengeance' or 'judicial payback' (ekdikesis) is reserved to God, and 'wrath' (orge) is given its proper object. Crucially the same root word family 'ekdik-' (the 'justice' or 'avenge' root) reappears as 'avenger' (ekdikos) in Romans 13:4, transferred onto the civil ruler, so the canon takes the very right that Romans 12:19 withholds from the believer and locates it in the state. This is the word-family pivot that holds both poles together and forbids collapsing either one.

'Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good' (me niko hupo tou kakou, alla nika en to agatho to kakon). Present-tense commands with 'by' (hupo, marking agency) and 'in/with' (en, marking instrument) frame the disciple's victory as moral, accomplished by good not by force. This caps the personal-ethic block immediately before the civil sphere appears in Romans 13:1.

'Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities' (pasa psyche exousiais hyperechousais hupotassestho), with the present passive command 'let him be subject' (hupotassestho) and the universal 'every soul' (pasa psyche), places every soul under the 'authorities' (exousiai). The clause 'and those that exist have been arranged under God' (hai de ousai hypo theou tetagmenai eisin) uses the perfect passive participle 'have been arranged' (tetagmenai, a past arrangement whose effect still stands) to assert a settled, prior ordering by God. The grammar leaves no creaturely sphere where 'authority' (exousia) is not under God's order, although it does not specify the believer's mode of participation.

'The one who sets himself against the authority has set himself against the ordinance of God' (ho antitassomenos te exousia te tou theou diatage anthesteken), with the perfect-tense 'has set himself against' (anthesteken, a completed action whose result still stands) and the participle 'those who have set themselves against' (anthestekotes), declares that resisting the authority resists God's ordinance and incurs 'judgment' (krima). The same 'against'-stem (anti-) word family that Matthew 5:39 prohibits in personal retaliation here describes culpable resistance to the governing power, and the shift in object (a personal evildoer versus an ordained authority) is the structural heart of the canonical tension.

The ruler is twice called 'God's servant' or 'minister' (theou diakonos) and is said to bear the 'sword' (machaira): 'for he does not bear the sword in vain, for he is God's servant, an avenger for wrath against the one who practices evil' (ou gar eike ten machairan phorei, theou gar diakonos estin, ekdikos eis orgen to katechorounti to kakon prassonti). 'In vain' (eike) plus the present-tense 'he carries' (phorei, habitually) frames the sword as a real, ongoing instrument of office, not a metaphor. The noun 'avenger' (ekdikos) is from the same word family as the 'vengeance' (ekdikesis) denied to the believer in Romans 12:19, so the same right is here vested in the civil officer. The text grounds a sphere where coercive force is divinely authorized, which materially complicates an absolute pacifist reading.

'Let the one who has none buy a sword' (ho me echon agorasato... machairan) instructs the one without a sword to buy one. The aorist-tense command 'let him buy' (agorasato, a completed-action imperative) is grammatically a real command, yet the disciples' production of two and Jesus's abrupt 'it is enough' (hikanon estin) in 22:38, plus the rebuke at the arrest in 22:51 and Matthew 26:52, pull against reading it as a standing mandate for armed force. The grammar permits both a literal reading and a figurative provisioning reading (the sword as symbolic preparation), and the saying is invoked by both sides without the words themselves resolving either.

'Soldiers' (strateuomenoi) ask 'what shall we do?' (ti poiesomen kai hemeis), and John answers 'extort from no one and do not falsely accuse, and be content with your wages' (medena diaseisete mede sykophantesete, kai arkeisthe tois opsoniois hymon). The participle 'soldiering' (strateuomenoi) is left intact, the prohibitions target extortion and intimidation, and 'wages' (opsoniois) names the soldier's pay. The grammar regulates how a soldier conducts himself; it does not require him to leave the office. This is one of the strongest New Testament data points for a continuing legitimacy of military vocation, although it does not by itself authorize the believer's participation.

'Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for in the image of God he made man' (shophek dam ha'adam ba'adam damo yishaphek, ki betselem Elohim asah et-ha'adam). The participle 'one who sheds' (shophek) is set against the passive 'shall be shed' (yishaphek), with the agent 'by man' (ba'adam) made explicit. The grounding clause 'for in the image of God' (ki betselem Elohim) ties capital justice to the 'image of God' (imago Dei, the Latin label for that doctrine). This places lethal civil sanction at the post-flood foundation of human community, prior to Israel and Sinai, which is why Romans 13:4 can claim creational warrant for the sword.

'Eye under eye, tooth under tooth, hand under hand, foot under foot' (ayin tachat ayin, shen tachat shen, yad tachat yad, regel tachat regel). The preposition 'under' or 'in place of' (tachat) sets the formula in a judicial code 'ordinances' (mishpatim) administered by judges, not in a private-revenge code. Read in its source context this is a proportional ceiling on civic punishment, which is exactly what Jesus's citation in Matthew 5:38 invokes before he addresses personal posture.

'If anyone is to be killed by the sword, by the sword he is to be killed. Here is the patient endurance and the faith of the saints' (ei tis en machaira apoktanthenai, auton en machaira apoktanthenai. Hode estin he hypomone kai he pistis ton hagion). The 'if-then' clause (a conditional construction) and the closing 'patient endurance' (hypomone) of the saints locate the church's posture under empire in patient endurance, not armed resistance. The verse reinforces Matthew 26:52 for the gathered church without removing Romans 13:4 from the civil sphere.

complicating_texts.resolution: The state's bearing of the 'sword' (machaira) as 'God's servant' (theou diakonos) and 'avenger for wrath' (ekdikos eis orgen) establishes a divinely sanctioned sphere of coercive force. Addressed by noting the sphere distinction in the immediate context: Romans 12:19 explicitly forbids the believer to perform 'vengeance' (ekdikesis) and reserves it to God, then 13:4 calls the civil officer 'avenger' (ekdikos). The shared root word family carries the same right from one agent to another within the same paragraph. The texts are not formally contradictory but locate force in different agents. The distinction does not by itself settle whether a believer may serve as that agent, which is exactly where the readings diverge.

The command 'let him buy a sword' (agorasato machairan) is read alongside 'it is enough' (hikanon estin) in 22:38, Jesus's 'put back the sword' (apostrepson ten machairan) and the proverb-like (gnomic) saying in Matthew 26:52, and the rebuke of sword use at the arrest in Luke 22:51. Addressed by treating the saying as a vivid signal of impending hostility plus a literary setup for the quotation 'he was reckoned with the lawless' (en anomois elogisthe) in 22:37, since the immediate two swords are called enough and lethal use is checked moments later. The grammar permits both a literal and a figurative provisioning reading, so it weakens rather than resolves either position.

The perfect-tense 'has set himself against' (anthesteken, a completed action whose result still stands) applied to resisting the 'authority' (exousia) uses the same 'against'-stem (anti-) word family that Matthew 5:39 prohibits in personal retaliation. Addressed by observing the different objects of the verb: in Romans 13:2 the object is God's ordained authority, in Matthew 5:39 it is the personal evildoer. The shared root across opposite relations is acknowledged as the structural reason the canon does not yield a single uncontested verdict.

John's instruction to 'soldiers' (strateuomenoi) regulates conduct without requiring exit from the office, and Acts 10 narrates a centurion received without rebuke of vocation. Addressed by noting that the imperative content (no 'extortion' (diaseio), no 'false accusation' (sykophanteo), contentment with 'pay' (opsonion)) targets abuse of military power, not the office itself. The non-rebuke is a real signal but it is an argument from silence about the office, not an explicit endorsement of lethal force by the believer.

'Those who take the sword will perish by the sword' (hoi labontes machairan en machaira apolountai) is gnomic (a proverb-like general truth) and stops the disciple's defensive use of force at the cost of Jesus's mission. Addressed by reading it under that immediate context, which a non-resistant reader extends to all disciples and a sphere-distinction reader restricts to private vigilantism (taking justice into one's own hands outside lawful office) that pre-empts magistrate authority. The grammar does not specify the scope.

variants.note: No variant units were supplied for the cited verses and the bundle marks 'not_in_ecm_scope' true. The SBLGNT (the Society of Biblical Literature Greek New Testament) marginal sigla (the editorial markers in the margin) in Matthew 5:39, 5:44, Matthew 26:52, Luke 22:36-38, Romans 12:19-21, and Romans 13:1-4 touch word order, minor pronoun forms, and the presence or absence of articular constructions (phrases with the article 'the'), but they do not alter the presence of the key terms 'to resist' (antistenai), 'sword' (machaira), 'vengeance' (ekdikesis), 'avenger' (ekdikos), 'keep loving' (agapate), or the love-of-enemies command. The verdict holds across plausible readings.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads 'do not resist the evil one' (me antistenai to ponero) in Matthew 5:39, the present-tense command 'keep loving your enemies' (agapate tous echthrous) in 5:44, the proverb-like (gnomic) saying 'those who take the sword will perish by the sword' (hoi labontes machairan en machaira apolountai) in Matthew 26:52, and the Romans 12:17-21 sequence forbidding 'evil for evil' (kakon anti kakou) and reserving 'vengeance' (ekdikesis) to God as a binding kingdom ethic for the disciple. Romans 13 is read as descriptive of God's use of civil powers and not as a mandate the believer may personally execute. Revelation 13:10's 'patient endurance' (hypomone) is taken as the church's standing posture.

Reads Romans 13:4, the ruler bearing the 'sword' (machaira) as 'God's servant' (theou diakonos) and 'avenger for wrath' (ekdikos eis orgen), with shared-root weight from Romans 12:19, as establishing a legitimate sphere of coercive justice that Genesis 9:6 grounds at creation prior to Israel. Limits Matthew 5:39 to private retaliation by attending to the sub-lethal personal examples and the second-person address, treats Luke 3:14 and the unrebuked centurion vocation in Acts 10 as continuity of military office, and reads Matthew 26:52 as a maxim against private vigilantism (taking justice into one's own hands) that pre-empts magistrate authority. Concludes a believer may participate in restraining evil through ordained authority.

Reads the personal commands as binding on the disciple in private capacity and the Romans 13 sword as binding on civic office, but treats the believer as living in both spheres with different ethics in each, so non-combatant service or restricted participation is the consistent application. The word forms (lemmas) support a sphere distinction without specifying overlap.

Holds that the 'against'-stem (anti-) word family appearing in Matthew 5:39 and Romans 13:2, the 'justice/avenge' root (ekdik-) traveling from Romans 12:19 to Romans 13:4, the 'sword' (machaira) appearing in Romans 13:4, Luke 22:36, Matthew 26:52, and Revelation 13:10, and Genesis 9:6 sitting under Romans 13:4 yield genuinely competing emphases that word-form analysis (morphology) alone does not reconcile. Faithful readers reach different defensible conclusions and the lexical (word-level) pattern is materially contested.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on whether the second-person prohibition in Matthew 5:39 and the disciple ethic of Romans 12:17-21 govern only personal retaliation or a comprehensive ethic for the believer in every role, and on whether the same person may bear the 'sword' (machaira) described in Romans 13:4. The principle of 'scripture interprets scripture' (analogia scripturae, the Latin label) is invoked because the readings differ precisely in how they harmonize personal disciple instructions with civil-office instructions inside one canon.

stem_audit.notes: The proposition does not preload a single verdict on the lexical (word-level) question of force, since it explicitly affirms that both just-war and pacifist positions are held by faithful readers, which matches the contested lexical pattern. The embedded clause about a community having historically leaned toward pacifism or non-combatant service is a sociological claim about a community that the lexical store cannot confirm or deny, so it is set aside. The verdict was derived only on the lexical question of whether the canon yields a single uncontested position on the believer and force.

lay_summary: The Greek and Hebrew put two ethics side by side and do not flatten them. In Matthew 5:39 Jesus says do not resist the evil one, using a form of the verb 'to set oneself against' (anthistemi) under a negative, with personal examples: a slap, a lawsuit, a forced mile. In 5:44 the present-tense command 'keep loving' (agapate) the enemy keeps loving them. In Matthew 26:52 Jesus tells his own disciple to put the sword (machaira) back, with the maxim that those who take the sword die by it. Romans 12 builds the same disciple ethic: never repay evil (kakon) for evil, leave room for God's wrath (orge), vengeance (ekdikesis) belongs to him, overcome evil with good. Read together these push toward refusing personal force. But the next sentence in Romans 13:4 calls the civil ruler God's servant (diakonos) who does not carry the sword (machaira) in vain, an avenger (ekdikos) who carries out wrath on the wrongdoer. Strikingly the very right Romans 12:19 takes from the believer (vengeance, ekdikesis) Romans 13:4 hands to the magistrate (avenger, ekdikos), same root word family, different agent. Genesis 9:6 puts capital justice into human hands at creation. The Old Testament eye for eye formula (lex talionis, a proportional-punishment rule) is judicial language for judges, not personal revenge. John the Baptist tells soldiers to stop extorting and live on their pay but does not tell them to quit. The same letter that forbids the believer to avenge calls the state an avenger, and the canon does not say in plain words whether one believer can occupy both roles. One careful reader says the disciple must never take up lethal force and that Romans simply describes God using worldly powers. Another careful reader says force belongs to a God-given civic sphere and that Matthew governs only private revenge. A third reader holds both, accepting civil sword in principle while declining personal combatant service. Because the canon supplies real warrant for more than one reading, and the words do not rank them, the lexical pattern here is contested rather than uniform.
